mood: The stock fell about two-thirds in 2022. Investors were angry about billions spent on the metaverse, and the company had just cut 11,000 jobs.
otherNews: It announced a $40bn share buyback, cut its 2023 cost forecast to $89–95bn (from $94–100bn), and called 2023 its 'year of efficiency'.
why: Profit missed badly, but investors were looking ahead. Lower costs and a huge buyback meant future profits per share would rise.

mood: Its crackdown on password sharing had added millions of new subscribers, and the stock had risen sharply over the past year. Investors expected another big quarter.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of $9.49bn, below the $9.54bn analysts expected, and said it would stop reporting subscriber numbers from 2025.
why: The quarter was great, but investors pay for future growth. A weak forecast and hiding subscriber numbers suggested the fast growth was slowing.

mood: The stock was hovering near multi-year lows heading into the print. Investors were deeply pessimistic, braced for a brutal 87% plunge in quarterly profits and an ongoing exodus of market share to fast-growing rivals.
otherNews: It warned that new tariffs could add costs of approximately $1bn.
why: The stock surged 15% in a single session after better-than-feared Q4 earnings. Investors found relief in early signs that the new CEO's plan to revive product innovation and repair wholesale relationships was taking hold.

mood: The stock had climbed about 34% since the start of August to a record high, and analysts were racing to keep up. It now traded at more than 200 times next year's expected profits, against about 35 for the biggest US tech companies.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of just over $1.3bn, ahead of the $1.2bn analysts expected, and raised its full-year forecast to $4.4bn from $4.15bn, despite fears the US government shutdown would hurt sales.
why: The results were excellent, but at that price investors already expected excellent. A beat and a raise couldn't justify paying even more, so the stock fell.

mood: Investors were cautious, fearing weak sales of its new phone, slow uptake of its new AI features, and China headwinds before earnings.
otherNews: It forecast only 'low to mid-single digit' sales growth for the holiday quarter, and said early sales of its newest phone were stronger than last year's model.
why: Apple reported a slight earnings beat alongside conservative low-to-mid single-digit revenue growth guidance for the upcoming holiday quarter. With no dramatic operational surprises to shift sentiment, the market reacted modestly.

mood: Investors avoided the stock, which fell over 35% by mid-2024, due to severe anxiety over market share losses to competitors and massive cash burn from its costly factory expansion.
otherNews: It said it would cut more than 15% of its staff, stop paying its dividend and cut $10bn of costs. For next quarter it forecast a loss of 3 cents a share on $12.5–13.5bn of revenue, while analysts expected a 31-cent profit on $14.35bn.
why: The results missed, the forecast was far below expectations, and scrapping the dividend and cutting 15% of staff showed how deep the trouble ran. Investors were worried because it had swung to a $1.61bn loss, rivals like AMD and Qualcomm were taking market share, and its data centre sales were shrinking. There was also a lack of immediate revenue because high upfront costs failed to pay off yet.

mood: Investors were anxious, weighing legal antitrust threats, generative AI search disruption, and heavy spending, leaving the underperforming stock range-bound.
otherNews: Its cloud business grew nearly 35% to $11.35bn on demand for its AI products, overall revenue grew 15%, and its new finance chief said it would keep cutting costs.
why: Although the company comfortably beat expectations behind strong core segment growth, ongoing regulatory pressure and surging capital spending limited broader investor enthusiasm.

mood: Investors were anxious and demanding, weighed down by sky-high expectations and fears that AI spending was nearing its peak. Despite a run of good news, the stock was up only about 5% for the year.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of $76.44–79.56bn, well above the $72.8bn analysts expected, and its gross margin rose to 75%.
why: Although the company beat estimates and raised guidance, a rally that had already priced in strong data centre demand and worries about how long AI spending could keep growing prompted profit-taking.

mood: Investors were optimistic as cost-cutting paid off and ad revenue rebounded, pushing the stock near all-time highs before earnings.
otherNews: It announced its first-ever dividend ($0.50 a share every quarter), added $50bn to its share buyback, and forecast next-quarter revenue of $34.6–37bn, above the $33.6bn analysts expected.
why: The company delivered a massive earnings blowout and initiated its first-ever dividend alongside a $50bn buyback, triggering a historic stock surge.

mood: Investors were optimistic yet demanding, driven by a strong year-to-date rally and expanding AI infrastructure partnerships alongside high valuation expectations.
otherNews: Its remaining performance obligations (contracted revenue it hasn't delivered yet) jumped 359% to $455bn, helped by four multibillion-dollar contracts. It forecast cloud infrastructure revenue of $18bn this year, rising to $144bn in four years.
why: A massive surge in remaining performance obligations and multi-billion-dollar cloud contract wins signaled overwhelming AI demand, triggering a violent upside breakout.

disguise: A big tech software and cloud company
mood: Investors were already uneasy as the stock lagged the market, harboring growing anxiety over massive capital expenditures and whether cloud revenue growth could justify the spending pace.
otherNews: It spent $37.5bn on data centres and equipment in the quarter, well above the $34.3bn expected. Its cloud business grew 39%, a little slower than the quarter before, and it forecast a slightly lower profit margin than analysts expected for next quarter.
why: Despite top and bottom-line beats, cloud revenue growth showed signs of deceleration while capital expenditure surged 66% to a record $37.5 billion, triggering fears of shrinking margins and delayed AI monetization.

disguise: A global retail and tech giant
mood: Investors were cautiously hopeful as deep workforce cuts boosted profitability, though persistent cloud growth deceleration kept enthusiasm restrained.
otherNews: Its profit jumped to $10.6bn from $278m a year earlier, ad sales beat expectations at $14.7bn, and it called the holiday season record-breaking. It forecast next-quarter revenue of $138–143.5bn, around the $142.1bn analysts expected.
why: Strong holiday sales, strong advertising growth, and massive profit margin expansion proved cost-cutting efforts paid off while cloud revenue stabilized.

mood: Investors were deeply discouraged following an underwhelming robotaxi unveiling, anxious over stagnating core sales and persistent profit margin erosion.
otherNews: Its CEO said his best guess was 20–30% vehicle growth next year, well above the roughly 15% analysts expected. Its car profit margin came in around 17%, ahead of the roughly 15% expected, though $739m of profit came from selling regulatory credits to other carmakers.
why: Although revenue missed estimates, an unexpected expansion in automotive gross margins and an aggressive forecast of up to 30% vehicle growth for the following year sparked a dramatic short squeeze.
